The question asked if Sub-Saharan Africa can cope with the benefits of the "test and treat" policy introduced by the World Health Organization (WHO). While the region is expected to benefit from this policy, there are concerns about its implementation and preparedness. The WHO's "test and treat" policy aims to accelerate the diagnosis and treatment of HIV/AIDS in the region.

However, the question went on to explore whether Sub-Saharan Africa has the capacity to manage any increased burden of antiretroviral therapy-related toxic and metabolic complications that may arise from implementing this policy. Experts emphasize the need for urgent measures to address these potential issues if SSA (Sub-Saharan Africa) is not prepared to handle the consequences.

Furthermore, questions were raised about whether combining antiretroviral agents in a single dosage form can enhance quality of life for HIV/AIDS patients. A study found that the cost-effectiveness of this approach was within the acceptable willingness-to-pay threshold, but the QALY (Quality-Adjusted Life Year) difference between treatments was minimal.

Additionally, concerns were raised about the dental health of new recruits to the British Armed Forces and whether there is a differential in dental health between these recruits. A study found that significant differences exist in dental health between recruits from different Services.

Other questions focused on whether gastric electrical stimulation (GES) is superior to standard pharmacologic therapy for improving gastrointestinal symptoms, healthcare resources, and long-term health care benefits. A review concluded that GES is more effective in reducing long-term GI symptoms, costs, and decreasing healthcare use compared to intensive medical therapy.

Lastly, there were questions about the distribution of health care benefits in Kenya and whether these meet the principles of universal coverage. A study found that the Kenyan health sector is inequitable and does not distribute benefits on the basis of need.

Overall, while Sub-Saharan Africa has made significant progress in reducing HIV/AIDS cases, concerns remain about its preparedness to implement the "test and treat" policy and manage any associated adverse effects.
